title: Geometry & Ornament Library
description: Studio cells, situated artifacts, comparisons, ornament episodes and reciprocal geometry–invention cases.

cells.name: Dot / point mark
cells.title: Dot / point mark
cells.geometry: A bounded mark representing a location; a drawn dot has area, unlike an ideal point.
cells.making: Place a mark with chosen pressure and repeat at intentional intervals.
cells.math: Position, distance, counting; point versus visible mark.
cells.rebuild: Place six marks at comparable intervals.
cells.redesign: Change spacing to create two focal groups.

cells.name: Line segment
cells.title: Line segment
cells.geometry: A straight bounded path joining two endpoints.
cells.making: Choose endpoints, rehearse the movement, then commit to a stroke.
cells.math: Length, orientation, parallelism, perpendicularity and intersection.
cells.rebuild: Draw a family between paired endpoints.

cells.name: Arc
cells.title: Arc
cells.geometry: A connected portion of a curve; this study selects circular arcs with an explicit center and radius.
cells.making: Make one continuous turning stroke or construct an arc; repeat its sweep.
cells.math: For circular arcs: radius, central angle, chord and arc length.
cells.observe: Identify where a boundary turns and stops.
cells.rebuild: Repeat one circular arc using a guide.
cells.redesign: Use related arcs to describe a rounded surface.

cells.name: Circle / disk
cells.title: Circle / disk
cells.geometry: A circle is the boundary at a fixed distance from a center; a disk includes the interior.
cells.making: Trace, freehand or compass-construct a closed boundary; compare outline and fill.
cells.math: Center, radius, diameter, circumference and area.
cells.rebuild: Make three circles with equal radii.
cells.redesign: Keep radii fixed while changing overlap and placement.

cells.name: Crescent
cells.title: Crescent
cells.geometry: A region between two curved edges; this exercise uses the difference of overlapping circular disks.
cells.making: Construct two circles and retain a selected crescent-shaped difference.
cells.math: Intersection, set difference, displacement and relative radii.
cells.observe: Compare both boundaries and the narrowest area.
cells.redesign: Vary only the offset and compare openings.

cells.title: Triangle
cells.geometry: A polygon with three straight sides and three vertices.
cells.making: Place three vertices, connect them, and compare the resulting area.
cells.rebuild: Keep a base fixed while varying height.
cells.redesign: Arrange triangular masses in a bounded field.

cells.name: Square / rectangular frame
cells.title: Square / rectangular frame
cells.geometry: A square has equal sides and right angles; rectangular framing is a related, distinct variant.
cells.making: Establish perpendicular edges and equal sides before subdividing.
cells.math: Parallelism, perpendicularity, ratios, area and subdivision.
cells.rebuild: Construct a square and divide it equally.
cells.redesign: Keep the outside fixed while changing interior divisions.

cells.name: Wave
cells.title: Wave
cells.geometry: A path with recurring rises and falls; a sinusoid is one model, not every wavy mark.
cells.making: Sustain repeated turns, using marked crest positions if helpful.
cells.math: Periodicity, amplitude and phase for an explicitly chosen model.
cells.rebuild: Draw four cycles at a chosen interval.
cells.redesign: Offset a second wave while preserving the first.

cells.name: Planar spiral
cells.title: Planar spiral
cells.geometry: A planar curve turns about a center while distance from that center changes by a chosen rule.
cells.making: Maintain a turning movement while controlling gaps between successive turns.
cells.math: Polar relationships; equal turn spacing differs from multiplicative radial growth.
cells.redesign: Fit the same rule inside two boundaries.

cells.name: Star / radial point motif
cells.title: Star / radial point motif
cells.geometry: A family of pointed radial constructions; alternating-radius outlines differ from regular star polygons and overlapping squares.
cells.making: Divide directions, alternate inner and outer points, and connect by the chosen rule.
cells.math: Angular division, rotational symmetry and polygon construction.
cells.observe: Count points and separate outer contour from interior intersections.
cells.redesign: Keep point count while changing the radius ratio.

cells.name: Hatch field
cells.title: Hatch field
cells.geometry: A family of strokes used together to build texture, value or surface direction.
cells.making: Repeat strokes with intentional intervals; change density or follow a surface.
cells.math: Spacing, density and local direction; freehand hatching need not have translation symmetry.
cells.observe: Compare dense and sparse areas and stroke direction.
cells.redesign: Wrap hatching around a form while controlling value.

cells.name: Crossed hatch field
cells.title: Crossed hatch field
cells.geometry: Overlapping stroke families whose intersections and densities build a composite field.
cells.making: Overlay a second family without losing control of its direction.
cells.math: Intersection angle, local subdivision and density; not inherently fractal.
cells.rebuild: Overlay two families at a chosen angle.
cells.redesign: Darken selected regions by adding one layer.

artifacts.title: Bowl
artifacts.technique: Dark painted decoration on ceramic; exact brush/tool construction unrecorded here
artifacts.rights: Public Domain (explicitly labeled on the object page)
artifacts.credit: Gift of Egypt Exploration Fund, by exchange, 1949
artifacts.source_attribution: The museum describes three concentric rings and three groups of double half-moons facing the center; its account says Ubaid painted pottery spread from southern Mesopotamia north and west.
artifacts.visible_observation: A shallow circular vessel bears dark bands following its inner rim and grouped, filled curved forms nearer the center. Cracks and oblique camera angle limit exact tracing.
artifacts.uncertainty: The page does not assign a lunar meaning to these half-moon motifs. A visual analogy with a crescent does not establish the same symbol as later Sin iconography.
artifacts.interpretation: Compare circular vessel structure with circular painted organization, and a small curved cell with its repeated arrangement.
artifacts.context: Excavated in Ubaid Cemetery, Grave 136, Eridu

artifacts.title: White cross-lined ware bowl with geometric patterns
artifacts.technique: Painted light lines on reddish pottery; exact production tools not identified by this record
artifacts.rights: Public Domain (explicitly labeled on the object page)
artifacts.source_attribution: The museum titles and dates the object as a Naqada I bowl with geometric patterns.
artifacts.visible_observation: Light bundles of angular strokes form repeated V- and W-like units down the wall, with long vertical strokes between fields. Individual marks are visibly freehand.
artifacts.uncertainty: No specific symbolic interpretation is supplied by the object record. Do not call the painted units a universal sign or infer transmission from similar chevrons.
artifacts.interpretation: A single line becomes an angular cell, then a repeated band; the curved vessel can host an emphatically angular design.
artifacts.context: Specific ancient use/find context not supplied in this record

artifacts.title: Jar (Hu)
artifacts.culture: China, Neolithic, Majiayao culture, Banshan phase
artifacts.place: Northwest China (museum audio identifies upper Yellow River basin)
artifacts.technique: Painted decoration; museum audio notes visible individual hand-painted brushstrokes
artifacts.rights: Public Domain (explicitly labeled on the object page)
artifacts.credit: Charlotte C. and John C. Weber Collection, Gift of Charlotte C. and John C. Weber, 1992
artifacts.source_attribution: Object details give Majiayao, Banshan phase and ca. 2650–2350 BCE.
artifacts.visible_observation: Bundles of curved dark and red lines sweep around circular unpainted centers across the broad shoulder. Angular forms occupy the neck, while the lower vessel remains largely unpainted.
artifacts.uncertainty: Use the object-details date. The audio transcript says second millennium BCE, inconsistent with those details; do not repeat that transcript date. Do not force curves into an exact named mathematical spiral.
artifacts.interpretation: Compare the same rounded host with Ubaid concentric organization and Egyptian angular repetition; contrast curved shoulder patterns against angular neck patterns within one work.
artifacts.context: Specific ancient use/find context not supplied in this record

artifacts.title: Cylinder seal and modern impression: worshiper and the sun god; king; bull-man and a lion-man
artifacts.technique: Carved cylinder intended for rolling impressions in clay
artifacts.rights: Public Domain (explicitly labeled on the object page)
artifacts.credit: Purchase, Raymond and Beverly Sackler Gift, 1991
artifacts.source_attribution: The museum identifies Shamash by the saw in his hand and describes a series of standing figures and smaller figures/items in the surrounding field.
artifacts.visible_observation: The cylinder is displayed beside a flattened modern impression. The impression presents a row of standing figures across a horizontal field.
artifacts.uncertainty: Main image is only 500 pixels wide, so fine marks should be studied from the museum source before detailed tracing. Geometry of rolling does not prove the ancient designer began with a flat sketch.
artifacts.interpretation: A strong contemporary comparison with the Old Syrian seal: similar date, same material and reproductive tool, different organization and iconographic selections.
artifacts.context: Museum explains sealing jars, doors, baskets and tablets as ownership/identification practices; modern impression shown

artifacts.title: Cylinder seal and modern impression: royal worshiper before a god on a throne; human-headed bulls below
artifacts.technique: Carved cylinder intended for rolling impressions in clay
artifacts.rights: Public Domain (explicitly labeled on the object page)
artifacts.credit: Purchase, Raymond and Beverly Sackler Gift, 1991
artifacts.source_attribution: Museum identifies a winged rosette disk with crescent, two stars, an ankh, a guilloche, and figures with Egyptian/Anatolian comparanda.
artifacts.visible_observation: A centrally placed disk and crescent appear above the figures; stars flank that area. Looping bands occupy side fields, and the composition stacks figures vertically as well as horizontally.
artifacts.uncertainty: Preserve local object attribution; museum-specified Egyptian elements are firmer evidence than resemblance alone. Not every star in every culture has the same deity or affective meaning.
artifacts.interpretation: Links cells, compound motifs, figural arrangement, tool geometry, and a specific cross-cultural iconographic combination without reducing the whole design to abstract geometry.
artifacts.context: Museum explains ownership/identification and transaction uses; modern impression shown

artifacts.title: Boundary stone (kudurru)
artifacts.place: South Babylonia; land grant in district of Edina
artifacts.institution: The British Museum (record published through Google Arts & Culture)
artifacts.rights: Photo: © Trustees of the British Museum. This record does not supply an explicit reuse license.
artifacts.credit: Photo: © Trustees of the British Museum
artifacts.source_attribution: Museum identifies Shamash with solar disk, Sin with crescent, and Ishtar with eight-pointed star; square boxes represent altars. It also identifies Marduk’s triangular spade and Nabu’s wedge-shaped stylus.
artifacts.visible_observation: Three large emblems occupy the arched upper field; smaller emblems sit on box-like bases below, above a cuneiform text block.
artifacts.uncertainty: Direct British Museum page returned 403; the BM-authored Google Arts & Culture record supplied these details. This is a legal-religious elite document, not evidence by itself for equal participation across society.
artifacts.interpretation: Connect geometry as iconography to legal material culture and represented tools: a triangle is simultaneously a geometric reading and part of a named spade emblem.
artifacts.context: Land grant by Eanna-shum-iddina to Gula-eresh; the record names surveyor and officials and invokes divine protection

artifacts.title: Luster Star-Shaped Tile
artifacts.medium: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque glaze with inglaze painting
artifacts.technique: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque glaze with inglaze painting
artifacts.rights: Public Domain, explicitly stated on object page
artifacts.credit: H.O. Havemeyer Collection, Gift of Horace Havemeyer, 1940
artifacts.source_attribution: The catalogue identifies a sultan with court members, framed by Persian poetry. The date is recorded on the tile.
artifacts.visible_observation: Eight-pointed star outline; border follows angular perimeter. Human figures occupy an interior field; fine curls fill multiple surface regions.
artifacts.interpretation: A useful layered case: geometric carrier + framed image + fine curvilinear ornament. The eight-point contour does not establish shared meaning with Mesopotamian astral stars.
artifacts.uncertainty: The source describes medium and luster process, not the exact tool or template used to lay out this outline.

artifacts.title: Mihrab (Prayer Niche)
artifacts.medium: Mosaic of polychrome-glazed cut tiles on stonepaste body; set into mortar
artifacts.technique: Mosaic of polychrome-glazed cut tiles on stonepaste body; set into mortar
artifacts.rights: Public Domain, explicitly stated on object page
artifacts.source_attribution: The museum identifies the niche as marking the direction of Mecca. Small glazed tiles are fitted together to form patterns and inscriptions.
artifacts.visible_observation: Nested rectangular frames surround a pointed arch and concave niche. Curved vegetal bands, polygonal arrangements, and inscriptions occupy different nested fields.
artifacts.interpretation: The physical tile can be a construction cell; the assembled ornament has larger reusable units. Architecture makes additional borders, corners, and curved surfaces available to design.
artifacts.uncertainty: This niche and the star tile belong to different centuries; no direct lineage is claimed.

artifacts.title: Parfleche
artifacts.rights: Open access: object page explicitly permits copying, modification and distribution without permission
artifacts.source_attribution: Cleveland supplies the Apsaalooke attribution and approximate date. Nelson-Atkins describes parfleches as light, weather-resistant containers used for transport in Plains and Plateau mobile lifeways; that context is from a different Lakota example.
artifacts.visible_observation: Two rectangular flap fields close at a central seam. Yellow and green triangular fields, pale diagonal bands, red accents, and dark outlines repeat across the folds.
artifacts.interpretation: Compare how folding and closure organize a design. This is a mobile-society case, not proof that its makers had never settled or lived outside colonial history.
artifacts.uncertainty: Do not transfer Lakota motif meanings to this Apsaalooke object. Do not infer symbolic content from triangular resemblance.

artifacts.title: Strawberry Thief
artifacts.date: c. 1936 impression of design introduced in 1883
artifacts.rights: Open access: object page explicitly permits copying, modification and distribution without permission
artifacts.source_attribution: The indigo-discharge process involved dyeing the whole cloth blue, bleaching, and block printing. The William Morris Gallery identifies the 1883 design as expensive to produce but commercially popular.
artifacts.visible_observation: Paired birds and flowers repeat over a densely filled ground. Local bilateral arrangements interlock with a larger repeating field; curling stems weave around figurative motifs.
artifacts.interpretation: Geometry need not be the depicted subject: repeat, reflection, spacing, and registration organize figurative ornament. Skilled repeat production can increase circulation while remaining expensive.
artifacts.uncertainty: The design dates to 1883; this collection example dates to about 1936. Commercial success does not establish equitable access or measured saturation.
artifacts.maker: Designer: William Morris; printed example is posthumous

artifacts.title: The Grammar of Ornament
artifacts.culture: British design publication; selected cross-cultural material
artifacts.rights: Public domain media, explicitly stated by NGA
artifacts.source_attribution: The volume has 100 chromolithographic plates. V&A connects Jones’s study of Alhambra decoration, experimentation with chromolithography, design education, and publication for designers unable to access the originals.
artifacts.visible_observation: The displayed plate separates ornament into vertical and horizontal panels. Bilateral vegetal units, scrolling curves, and repeated motifs are arranged for comparison.
artifacts.interpretation: A sourcebook itself becomes an invention/host carrying copied geometries to new makers and media. Its historical selections and cultural labels remain the author’s framework, not a neutral global canon.
artifacts.uncertainty: The volume’s cultural taxonomy and selections belong to its nineteenth-century author, not a neutral global canon.
artifacts.maker: Owen Jones, author; Francis Bedford, lithographer

claims.text: Cleveland supplies the Apsaalooke attribution and approximate date. Nelson-Atkins describes parfleches as light, weather-resistant containers used for transport in Plains and Plateau mobile lifeways; that context is from a different Lakota example.
Two rectangular flap fields close at a central seam. Yellow and green triangular fields, pale diagonal bands, red accents, and dark outlines repeat across the folds.
Compare how folding and closure organize a design. This is a mobile-society case, not proof that its makers had never settled or lived outside colonial history.

claims.text: The indigo-discharge process involved dyeing the whole cloth blue, bleaching, and block printing. The William Morris Gallery identifies the 1883 design as expensive to produce but commercially popular.
Paired birds and flowers repeat over a densely filled ground. Local bilateral arrangements interlock with a larger repeating field; curling stems weave around figurative motifs.
Geometry need not be the depicted subject: repeat, reflection, spacing, and registration organize figurative ornament. Skilled repeat production can increase circulation while remaining expensive.

cycles.title: Cylinder, impression, circulation, new reading
stages: Rolling over clay makes a planar impression
Impressions identify ownership/authority on closures and transaction documents
evidenced: Rolling over clay makes a planar impression
Impressions identify ownership/authority on closures and transaction documents
proposed: A flat drawing can prototype a cylindrical design (modern exercise; ancient sketch stage not established here)

cycles.math: For an ideal cylinder rolling without slipping, one revolution advances a length equal to its circumference, 2πr; the unwrapped lateral surface is a rectangle of height h and length 2πr. This is a geometric model, not an exact measurement of these objects.
cycles.limits: The host invention is also the production tool here; pottery and architecture may instead be receiving surfaces.
cycles.reciprocal_question: How does a cylindrical carrier shape the scene, and how might a desired continuous scene shape carrier choice?
cycles.saturation_status: Unmeasured; requires evidence from sealing corpora.

activities.title: One cell, three roles, two carriers
activities.observe: Choose a vessel. Identify a stroke, a repeated unit and a larger arrangement. Separate visible marks from your proposed construction.
activities.rebuild: Make one neutral cell on paper and rebuild a short arrangement. Retain the layers. Wrap a copy around a paper cylinder and compare spacing and seam.
activities.redesign: Keep one geometric condition fixed and change one variable. Describe both the visual change and the making action.
activities.readiness: Record observation, tool execution and design choice independently. No fixed ages or measured learning gains are claimed.
activities.fge_note: F(ge) of the making action remains distinct from M(ge) of the image. A classroom construction does not establish an ancient procedure.
